doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: What a musical director must do on the road
summary: Writing simple charts for unknown local bands, the Melody Fair example, and the management handling logistics and music cases.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It was a thrill, yeah. It really worked out. I did learn a couple of other things along the way, in talking about what a musical director has to do. Sometimes you have to write a chart and you don’t know what the band is going to be like. So when you’re dealing with studio musicians or the LA Tonight Show Band or Vegas musicians, you can’t lose, because no matter what you do, even if you screw up they fix it for you. I mean they’re like really cool. But sometimes you get musicians that aren’t quite as experienced, and if you write something that’s too difficult to read, they don’t want to play it. So you look at it this way, if you write a bunch of whole and half notes when you can get away with it, and maybe a few figures, guys are going to look at that and say hey, I can do this. And you give the rhythm section most of the stuff because they’re rehearsed, they know what they’re doing, and the rest of it is sweetening. So for road musicians, at least back in those days, if you do it that way you’re going to have a pretty good show most of the time, even if they’re musicians that don’t get a chance to play that much — school teachers, whatever. In some towns, we had that situation in Buffalo. We played the Melody Fair in North Tonawanda. And the band was kind of like not really all that great. And so they had a couple of songs that they knew how to play by themselves, so they played the opening and then they kind of basically sat there tacet while we played the show self-contained, there was really maybe one or two charts that were real easy that they could do, and then they played the exit music, which was theirs, and that’s kind of what we did. Because it was just too much. But the whole trick is if you can make it look easy enough, most of the time they can do it on site, you’re going to be okay. If you make it look difficult you’re going to have a band that’s a little bit afraid to play the stuff and you’re not going to get a committed performance out of them.
Were you, did you have the responsibility of calling the local contractor yourself before you get to that town, or the manager did that or what?

No. In terms of Lou Rawls’ band there was a manager and a management company, and so all we had to do — and a travel agent and all that stuff. I mean in some bands you’ve got to do that too, you’ve got to call the airlines even. No this was, everything was handled, all we had to do was show up, and the hardest part of my job was carrying the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
four boxes of music — this and this and this — and make sure that they didn’t get lost with the airlines. We had situations where the music doesn’t show up.
Did you copy your own parts?
Did you copy your own parts at that time? Were you the copyist also?
